scenario: Today's thread in this track is how to adapt a robot policy to new conditions by changing only a small piece instead of retraining the large model. RAGu and GUARD both freeze the original policy and correct actions during generation with an outside signal, one using retrieved trajectories and the other an anomaly score of how far a state is from the training data. SFF refits only the last layer of a failure monitor online, and after deployment Rho likewise updates only a small module. REMAC and Thermo-VLA add a small change through LoRA or residuals, handling inference delay and the new thermal modality respectively.

papers.title: Real-Time Robot Execution with Masked Action Chunking
papers.authors: Haoxuan Wang, Gengyu Zhang, Yan Yan, Yuzhang Shang, Ramana Rao Kompella, Gaowen Liu
papers.abstract:
Real-time execution is essential for cyber-physical systems such as robots. These systems operate in dynamic real-world environments where even small delays can undermine responsiveness and compromise performance. Asynchronous inference has recently emerged as a system-level paradigm for real-time robot manipulation, enabling the next action chunk to be predicted while the current one is being executed. While this approach achieves real-time responsiveness, naive integration often results in execution failure.
Previous methods attributed this failure to inter-chunk discontinuity and developed test-time algorithms to smooth chunk boundaries. In contrast, we identify another critical yet overlooked factor: intra-chunk inconsistency, where the robot’s executed action chunk partially misaligns with its current perception. To address this, we propose REMAC, which learns corrective adjustments on the pretrained policy through masked action chunking, enabling the policy to remain resilient under mismatches between intended actions and actual execution during asynchronous inference. In addition, we introduce a prefix-preserved sampling procedure to reinforce inter-chunk continuity.
Overall, our method delivers more reliable policies without incurring additional latency. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that our method enables faster task execution, maintains robustness across varying delays, and consistently achieves higher completion rates.
papers.scoring_note: REMAC real-time deployment; simulation and real hardware, delay robustness and ACT extension
papers.summary: Running the next model call while the robot executes the current action segment is meant to avoid pauses, yet done naively it lowers success. Earlier work blamed poor joins between consecutive segments. The authors point to an overlooked cause: by the time the model finishes, the robot has already taken a few steps from the old plan, so the first steps of the new segment never run, yet training still supervises them. REMAC randomly masks the first several steps of each segment in training, computes loss only on the part that will run, and learns a LoRA correction that is merged back before inference, adding no latency. Under the largest delay in simulation, success rises from 0.451 to 0.779. ==Inference delay is a known condition, so building it into training beats patching at inference time==.

papers.title: Runway’s Praxis-1 world action model for robotics is now available
papers.abstract:
Runway launched Praxis-1 with partners including Noble Machines, Standard Bots, and Ultra. Developers can now use it with open weights.

The post Runway’s Praxis-1 world action model for robotics is now available appeared first on The Robot Report.
papers.scoring_note: Open weights Apache2; three embodiments; 46.2% RoboLab and 15/15 plank trials
papers.summary: Runway, a video generation company, has turned its video foundation model into a robot policy called Praxis-1, released with open weights under Apache 2.0 along with inference and fine-tuning code. It is a 27B-parameter MoE diffusion Transformer that predicts upcoming frames and robot actions together. Video prediction stays in training throughout, so the model predicts the scene's next frame and then outputs the motion that gets there. Runway says web video matches teleoperated robot video as pretraining data. On RoboLab-120 it reaches 46.2% success, against 28.0% for π0.5. ==If that holds, the data bottleneck for robot policies becomes how much general video a model can learn from==.

papers.title: Zero-Shot VLA Adaptation with Retrieved Guidance
papers.authors: Subin Kim, Anh-Quan Pham, Dinesh Jayaraman
papers.abstract: Pre-training large parametric "Vision-Language-Action" (VLA) models on large demonstration datasets has recently yielded promising results for general-purpose manipulation. However, these models still struggle under even small domain shifts relative to the training data, such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity, or robot morphology. Motivated by the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in language models, we pursue retrieval to boost VLA performance. Specifically, we seek to leverage retrieval from domain-mismatched, "in-the-wild" demonstration datasets like DROID to guide a VLA's behavior in a new target domain. To achieve this, we introduce RAGu, which overcomes robotics-specific challenges for RAG: (1) It incorporates simple geometric calibration to transform source demonstrations into the target setup and reduce cross-domain differences. (2) It uses a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy that selects, from a large pool of pre-warped candidates, the trajectory most compatible with the base VLA. (3) It guides the VLA's flow-matching inference procedure rather than seeking to retrain the base model or expand its limited context window. We evaluate RAGu across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real transfer, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation. We find it improves real-world VLA success rates from 20% to 80% and outperforms the closest-related baselines in sim. Project website: raguvla.github.io
papers.scoring_note: Individual original-abstract assessment; no preference bonus; niche domains and sensor/control-only work calibrated separately.
papers.summary: Concatenating retrieved demonstrations into the model context is the standard RAG recipe for language models, but it does not carry over to robots. The authors retrieve demonstrations from real data such as DROID, whose viewpoints and objects do not match the target scene, and the context-concatenation baseline never succeeds on the real robot, doing worse than no retrieval. RAGu first warps the retrieved trajectories geometrically to the object positions in the target scene, then picks the one requiring the least change to the model's own actions. While the model generates actions, they are corrected toward that trajectory, with weights and context untouched. Real-robot success rises from 20% to 80%. ==Retrieved results need not enter the context; they can also guide generation==.

papers.title: Spatial Representation Distillation and Knowledge Routing for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Jungin Park, Chaoran Zhu, Changjae Oh, Kwanghoon Sohn
papers.abstract: Understanding three-dimensional physical structure has become essential for vision-language-action models (VLAs). However, existing approaches either rely on explicit geometric inputs at inference time or adopt a single visual pathway, potentially compromising the visual-semantic knowledge inherited from pre-trained models. We present SPARK-VLA, Spatial Representation distillation and Knowledge routing for VLAs, a preserve-specialize-route framework for spatially adapting VLAs without requiring external 3D inputs or experts at inference. SPARK-VLA consists of two key components: (1) spatial representation distillation, which transfers 3D understanding from a frozen 3D expert to a LoRA-adapted visual branch by aligning attention responses while preserving the original visual pathway, and (2) a lightweight knowledge router, which selectively forwards action-relevant visual tokens to the language model using routing supervision derived from action-loss gradients. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and real-world manipulation, SPARK-VLA achieves strong performance with only a 0.5B language backbone and approximately 53M trainable parameters, providing an effective and parameter-efficient approach to 3D-aware VLA learning. Code is available at https://github.com/park-jungin/spark-vla.
papers.scoring_note: Individual original-abstract assessment; no preference bonus; niche domains and sensor/control-only work calibrated separately.
papers.summary: To give a VLA 3D understanding, one either feeds extra depth maps or point clouds at inference or trains 3D knowledge into the original visual encoder, which can damage the general visual ability from pretraining. SPARK-VLA keeps the original visual pathway and opens a second LoRA pathway beside it, which learns from a frozen 3D model, VGGT, during training; VGGT is not needed at inference. Each pathway yields one token per image position, and a small router decides from the instruction which ones go to the language model. The router's labels come from the gradient of the action loss with respect to each token, and tokens that lower the action error count as useful. In an ablation, concatenating all tokens gives 94.0% success, while routed selection gives 98.0%. ==With several feature sources, selecting beats passing everything==.

papers.title: Thermo-VLA: A Thermal-Aware Vision-Language-Action Model with Gated Residual Modulation for Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Jingxuan Chen, Junshi Luo, Chencheng Dong, Xiaojian Nie, Tongge Huang, Qiang Huang
papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have begun incorporating thermal sensing, but existing approaches typically treat thermal images as ordinary visual inputs, providing limited support for temperature-aware relational reasoning in manipulation. To address this limitation, we propose Thermo-VLA with a ThermoRes Encoder, which decomposes thermal images into cold and hot attribute representations and injects them into the RGB token through language-conditioned residual modulation, enabling temperature-driven target selection and continuous manipulation. We further construct six real-world robotic tasks on a dual-arm Unitree G1 platform, spanning basic grounding to relational reasoning. Experiments show that Thermo-VLA achieves an average success rate of 0.86 across four thermal-dependent tasks, outperforming a pi_0.5 baseline that directly incorporates RGB-thermal observations by 18 percentage points. Under unseen-object and scene variations, Thermo-VLA maintains an average success rate of 0.78, achieving the best generalisation performance among the compared methods. Beyond thermal sensing, we transfer the same residual modulation mechanism to colour attributes and observe consistent improvements in both simulation and real-robot experiments, indicating its potential to generalise beyond thermal attributes. Project website: https://j-x-chen.github.io/Thermo-VLA-web/
papers.scoring_note: Individual original-abstract assessment; no preference bonus; niche domains and sensor/control-only work calibrated separately.
papers.summary: Some tasks require picking objects by temperature, such as removing the cage holding a dead mouse that is no longer warm, which an ordinary camera cannot tell apart, so thermal imaging is needed. Existing approaches feed the thermal image to the VLA as just another picture and succeed only about half the time on this task, often grabbing a salient heat source. Thermo-VLA uses the background temperature as a reference to split the thermal image into views colder and hotter than the background, weights the two by the instruction text, and adds them as residuals onto the RGB tokens, leaving the RGB representation intact. Across four temperature-dependent tasks it averages 0.86 success, 18 percentage points above π0.5 with thermal input added directly. ==Injecting a new modality as instruction-weighted residuals interferes least with existing visual ability==.

papers.title: Streaming Failure Forecasting: VLA Failure Monitors That Keep Learning After Deployment
papers.authors: Amit Jadhav, Shaurya Beriwala, David Q. Liu, Yanfei Liu
papers.abstract: Failure monitors for vision-language-action (VLA) policies are trained offline and then frozen. After deployment, lighting, objects and cameras drift, and the policy itself is updated or moved to new tasks. On recorded real-robot runs, after a switch of task or policy version, a frozen monitor fit on the old task ranks failures little better than chance. We present Streaming Failure Forecasting (SFF), a monitor that keeps learning from the one label every episode provides: whether it succeeded. SFF keeps the offline monitor's network fixed and refits only its last linear layer after each episode, at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core. Its alarm threshold moves only after successes, which in simulation kept false alarms near target except when two drifts came at once. With every setting locked before testing, SFF ranks failures better than the same monitor kept frozen on 4 of 5 simulated test suites under unannounced drift, and above resetting on detected drift on every suite. Carried with its locked learner settings to 434 recorded runs of four VLAs on real SO-101 arms, replayed across unannounced switches of task or policy version, it ranks failures better than the frozen monitor for every VLA and, in an exploratory comparison, above a full reset at the true switch. A deployed failure monitor need not stay frozen: refitting its readout from outcomes is cheap and helps after the changes we tested.
papers.scoring_note: Individual original-abstract assessment; no preference bonus; niche domains and sensor/control-only work calibrated separately.
papers.summary: After deployment, lighting, objects and cameras change, and the policy gets updated or moved to new tasks, yet the failure monitor is usually trained offline and then frozen. On real-robot runs of four VLAs, the authors find that once the task or policy version switches, the frozen monitor ranks failures barely better than chance. SFF's fix is cheap: the monitor network stays fixed, and after every episode the last linear layer is refit in closed form from one label, whether the episode succeeded. The alarm threshold is tuned separately and moves only after successes, to hold down false alarms. On 434 real-robot runs, the AUROC for ranking failures rises from 0.536 when frozen to 0.656. ==Ranking comes from refitting the last layer online, false alarms from a separate threshold==, the same idea as freezing a recommender backbone and updating only its last layer online.

papers.title: UniLatent: Cross-Embodiment Transfer via Latent Observation Alignment
papers.authors: Yufei Ding, Yi Du, Weiduo Yuan, Hao Jiang, Dylan Goetting, Lawrence Yunliang Chen, Daniel Seita, Yue Wang
papers.abstract: Robot datasets are costly to collect and are usually tied to a specific embodiment, making it difficult to reuse demonstrations across robots with different geometry, appearance, and kinematics. We introduce UniLatent, a cross-embodiment transfer framework that reduces the embodiment-induced observation gap in a shared latent space. UniLatent renders paired source-target robot observations in simulation and aligns a source visual encoder to a frozen target encoder. A policy trained on encoded source demonstrations can then run directly on target observations, with no pixel-level image translation. Across three simulation tasks and two target robot arms, UniLatent reaches up to 93% zero-shot success, exceeding the strongest pixel-translation baseline by over 30 points on average. In real-world xArm-to-Franka transfer, fine-tuning with only 10 target demonstrations per task yields 27/30 successful rollouts. Code, videos and data are available at https://selina2023.github.io/unilatent/.
papers.scoring_note: Individual original-abstract assessment; no preference bonus; niche domains and sensor/control-only work calibrated separately.
papers.summary: Robot demonstration data is expensive and tied to one specific arm. Switch arms and the arm's shape and occlusions in the image change, so the policy stops working. The usual fix repaints the source robot frame by frame into the target robot, but repainting leaves artifacts, and the policy learns them too. UniLatent aligns in representation space instead: in simulation it poses both arms at the same end-effector pose, renders paired images, and trains the source robot's visual encoder so its embedding matches the frozen target encoder. The policy trains on embeddings of the source data and at deployment reads the target robot's images directly. In simulation, mean success rises from 44.5% with the strongest repainting baseline to 76.0%. ==Aligning in representation space sidesteps the artifacts of repainting pixels==.

papers.title: ReSkill: Selective Self-Improvement for Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Zheng Sun, Zhihao Li, Zhuo Li, Wenrui Liu, Xin Wang, Fei Chen
papers.abstract: Self-improvement on compositional manipulation tasks requires deciding what to reuse, where to improve, and which changes to retain. We present ReSkill, a selective self-improvement framework that concentrates revision on capability gaps. A coding agent constructs an object-centric task graph from an instruction and a skill library, then uses node-level execution records to locate failures. At the task level, it revises stage organization, hand-off conditions, and recovery routes; at the skill level, it strengthens perception, motion, manipulation, and verification capabilities that repeatedly fail. Candidate revisions undergo full-task evaluation and paired comparisons before adoption, allowing local changes to accumulate into validated skills and an independently executable policy. The agent participates only during development; the deployed policy calls the retained skills without invoking the agent at run time. On the same development set, average success across ten RoboDojo tasks rises from 30.0% for the initial versions to 86.2% for the final adopted programs; retained programs achieve 83.6% in recorded robustness and model-selection evaluations. Across eight real-world tasks, ReSkill succeeds in 72 of 80 rebuilt-simulation trials and 62 of 80 real-robot trials (77.5%). The median revision changes only three functions, approximately 0.5% of a program, while 39% of task-specific functions in later-added tasks directly reuse existing implementations. These results show how locating local deficiencies, validating candidate changes, and accumulating reusable skills can improve execution of compositional manipulation tasks.
papers.scoring_note: Individual original-abstract assessment; no preference bonus; niche domains and sensor/control-only work calibrated separately.
papers.summary: When a robot meets a new multi-step task, it usually fails at only a few steps, so retraining everything is wasteful. ReSkill has a coding agent break the task, during development, into an object-centric task graph in which each node calls a skill. The agent uses each node's execution records to find the failing step and revises only the flow or skill there. Every change must run on the full development layouts and win a paired comparison with the current version before it is kept. At deployment the robot runs only the revised program and never calls the agent. Across ten simulated tasks, average success rises from 30.0% for the initial versions to 86.2%, and the median revision changes only three functions. ==The large model only edits programs during development; production runs fixed code==.

papers.title: GUARD: Anomaly-Informed Q-Steering for Generative Robot Policies in Dexterous Manipulation
papers.authors: Aryaman Gupta, Xiaoyue Wu, Rana Soltani Zarrin, Mark Van der Merwe
papers.abstract: Generative robot policies based on diffusion and flow matching can model complex, multimodal behaviors, but remain susceptible to covariate shift during closed-loop execution. Existing approaches mitigate such failures through additional demonstrations, policy fine-tuning, or test-time guidance, but often require human intervention, engineered rewards, or other task-specific signals. We introduce GUARD, an anomaly-informed Q-steering framework that leverages the policy's training distribution to construct a dense, failure-anticipatory steering signal. GUARD pairs sparse task rewards with dense anomaly scores learned from policy training data and propagates both through a learned Q-function. Its gradients then steer the denoising process toward actions that improve task return while preventing trajectories from entering poorly supported regions, without directly modifying the pretrained policy. Across four Adroit dexterous manipulation tasks, GUARD achieves average success rates of $96.0\%$ and $80.0\%$ under nominal and perturbed dynamics, outperforming the strongest baseline by $21.0$ and $20.0$ percentage points while maintaining the lowest anomaly score. GUARD further demonstrates direct sim-to-real transfer on in-hand screwdriver rotation and reorientation tasks, achieving $40$ and $25$ percentage-point gains in success rate. These results demonstrate that anomaly signals can serve not only for failure monitoring but also to complement sparse task rewards as effective supervision for robust policy steering.
papers.scoring_note: Individual original-abstract assessment; no preference bonus; niche domains and sensor/control-only work calibrated separately.
papers.summary: Robot policies trained with diffusion or flow matching tend to fail once execution drifts into states the training data did not cover, and the task reward is usually just final success, too late to correct course. GUARD learns an anomaly score from the policy's training data that measures how far the current state is from that data, treats it as a dense per-step reward, and trains a Q-function on it together with the sparse success reward. During action generation, the Q-function's gradient corrects the denoising, pushing actions toward completing the task without leaving the training distribution, while the policy weights stay unchanged. On four dexterous-hand tasks average success is 96.0%, and using the success reward alone scores 30 percentage points lower. ==Distance from the training distribution is a ready-made dense reward==.

papers.title: Rho: A Foundation for Efficiently Adaptable VLA Models
papers.abstract: General-purpose physical AI models must combine broad visual and linguistic capabilities with precise control across robot embodiments and efficient adaptation to downstream tasks. We introduce Rho, a family of open-weights VLA models for bimanual manipulation designed for data-light task adaptation on 3 embodiments representative of dual-arm robots across research labs and the industry -- YAM Box, UR AI Trainer, and FR3 Duo. We systematically ablate Rho's action-expert architecture and training recipe, and show in controlled simulation and physical-robot experiments that embodiment midtraining improves downstream adaptation. The resulting Rho variants for YAM Box, UR AI Trainer, and FR3 Duo match or outperform existing open-weights VLAs and achieve the strongest overall performance across the tasks, embodiments, and baselines evaluated in this report. We further demonstrate the Rho model family's built-in capacity for online adaptation: an internal latent policy learns from corrective feedback to select observation-conditioned noise inputs for the frozen flow-matching action expert. With as few as 15 corrected episodes, adapting this lightweight module enables Rho to handle task situations at the fringe of its offline finetuning distribution. Together, these results position Rho as both a strong general-purpose robotic manipulation model and a practical foundation for adaptation. We release the base Rho model and the embodiment-specific checkpoints to facilitate Rho's deployment in research experiments and practical industrial use cases.
papers.authors: Rho Team, Simran Bagaria, Daphne Chen, Dean Fortier, Jianlong Fu, Michael Harrison, Tess Hellebrekers, Neel Joshi, Andrey Kolobov, Dalton Moore, Galen Mullins, Michael Murray, Eduardo Salinas, Reuben Tan
papers.scoring_note: Open weights, three physical embodiments, adaptation with 15 corrected episodes
papers.summary: Microsoft has released Rho, an open-weights family of VLAs for dual-arm manipulation. Its core finding is that inserting an intermediate stage between general pretraining and task fine-tuning, trained on many tasks for one specific robot and called midtraining by the authors, halves the data needed for later task fine-tuning. The paper's explanation is that pretraining sees many robots but learns each shallowly, so learning a new task directly also means learning to control that robot. On a real FR3 Duo dual-arm setup, with the same plug-insertion training budget, success rises from 60.0% without midtraining to 86.7% after two midtraining epochs. ==Splitting robot adaptation from task adaptation makes the task step cheap==, the same logic as domain continual pretraining before business fine-tuning in recommendation.
